title: The small holocaust, 1746
hookLine: thousands of Sikhs are killed in a campaign near Kahnuwan
tomorrow: The Dal Khalsa and the council

cards: Some families have a year nobody mentions lightly. The year of the flood, the fire, the war.
The older relatives lower their voices when it comes up, and the children learn, without being told, that this is something you remember carefully.

The Sikh community has two years like that in the eighteenth century, and they have names. The first came in 1746, in the marshes and hills of northern Punjab. Today: Chhota Ghallughara, the small holocaust.

teach.b: Ghallughara is the Punjabi word Sikhs use for a massacre, a great destruction. Chhota means small, only because a larger one would come sixteen years later.
In 1746 Lakhpat Rai, a senior official in Lahore, lost his brother in a clash with a Sikh band, and swore to wipe out the Sikhs in return. First, Sikhs living in Lahore were rounded up and killed.
Then he led a large army, with cannon, to the marshy forest of Kahnuwan, near the Beas and Ravi rivers. Thousands of Sikhs were camped there: fighters, along with women, children and old people.

teach.h: TRAPPED BETWEEN ARMY, RIVER AND HILLS.
teach.b: They fled north toward the hills, hoping for shelter, and were trapped between the soldiers behind them, a swollen river, and hill rulers who wouldn't let them in.
Over several weeks in the early summer, thousands were killed, and many who were captured were taken to Lahore and executed.
The numbers in the old accounts vary, often around seven thousand killed and three thousand captured. Nobody knows exactly.

Sikhs don't tell this story to stir up hatred. The people who did this are long gone, and no one living today carries the blame. They tell it so the people who died aren't forgotten, and because of what came next.
The survivors regrouped. Within a few years they were stronger and better organized than before. That's tomorrow's story.

how: Sikhs remember the Chhota Ghallughara of 1746 in their histories and at gurdwaras, and the martyrs of the eighteenth century are named in general terms in Ardas, the daily prayer.

practice: A minute of silence: sit still, hands resting, with nothing to imagine and nothing in particular to feel.
Just hold a quiet space for people you'll never know, who were lost that summer, and for anyone, anywhere, whose family carries a year like that. If you pray, let the silence be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Chhota Ghallughara. The small holocaust of 1746, when thousands of Sikhs were killed in a campaign near Kahnuwan. Remembered, not turned to hate.
